bacterial_leaf_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked to yellowish-white stripes starting along leaf margins, progressing lengthwise with wavy edges. Lesions turn grayish-white as tissues die. Bacterial ooze beads may emerge in high humidity.
bacterial_leaf_blight.causes: Bacterium enters through natural openings (hydathodes) or mechanical wounds from storms and transplanting.
bacterial_leaf_blight.favorable_conditions: High temperatures (25-34°C), relative humidity >70%, heavy monsoon rainfall, and excessive nitrogenous fertilizer application.
prevention: Plant certified resistant or tolerant rice varieties.
Maintain balanced fertilization; avoid excess basal or top-dressed nitrogen.
Ensure field sanitation by plowing under stubbles and removing wild host grasses.
management: Drain standing water temporarily to lower canopy humidity.
Spray recommended copper hydroxide or validamycin as advised by local extension officers.
Disinfect harvesting and threshing equipment between fields.
bacterial_leaf_blight.consult_expert_when: Symptoms spread rapidly over >20% of canopy during tillering or panicle initiation.
bacterial_leaf_blight.references: International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) Rice Knowledge Bank; ICAR-CRRI Rice Disease Guide.

brown_spot.symptoms: Small, circular to oval sesame seed-shaped spots with dark brown margins and gray or whitish centers across leaf blades.
brown_spot.causes: Airborne fungal conidia; strongly associated with poor soil fertility, zinc/potassium deficiency, or drought stress.
brown_spot.favorable_conditions: Temperatures of 20-30°C, prolonged leaf wetness (>16 hours), drought or unflooded soil conditions.
prevention: Treat seed with hot water (53-54°C for 10-12 mins) or certified seed dressers before sowing.
Apply recommended potassium, silicon, and micronutrients based on soil testing.
Avoid severe water stress during early vegetative stages.
management: Improve irrigation to prevent soil drying out.
Apply foliar potassium spray to revitalize stressed tillers.
Use biocontrol agents such as Trichoderma harzianum or consult local extension for fungicides.
brown_spot.consult_expert_when: Spots coalesce leading to extensive leaf blight and seedling damping-off.
brown_spot.references: IRRI Diagnostic Guide; FAO Rice Production Compendium.

leaf_smut.symptoms: Small, slightly raised, angular black spots on both leaf surfaces. The lesions remain distinct and covered by the epidermis.
leaf_smut.causes: Fungal chlamydospores overwintering on infected crop residue.
leaf_smut.favorable_conditions: High humidity, mature crop canopy, and moderate warmth.
prevention: Crop rotation with non-host legumes.
Deep plowing of post-harvest crop debris.
Use certified clean seeds.
management: Usually minor; rarely requires chemical spray if balanced fertilizer is used.
Ensure good airflow across rows by maintaining recommended plant spacing.
leaf_smut.consult_expert_when: Co-infection with blast or bacterial blight occurs simultaneously.
leaf_smut.references: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture Rice Diseases; IRRI.

healthy.symptoms: Vibrant green, uniform leaf blades without necrotic spots, discoloration, or bacterial lesions.
healthy.causes: Optimal nutrient management, proper water depth, and absence of active pathogen pressure.
prevention: Continue regular scouting, monitor water levels, and follow integrated pest management protocols.
management: Maintain balanced N-P-K nutrition and scout weekly during panicle development.
healthy.consult_expert_when: Inspect foliage promptly if unexpected wilting or yellowing appears.
healthy.references: AgriGuard Agronomic Advisory; IRRI Standard Operating Procedures.

apple_scab.symptoms: Dull olive-green to black velvety spots on leaf surfaces. Spots become puckered and distorted as leaf expands.
apple_scab.causes: Overwinters in fallen dead apple leaves; releases ascospores during spring rainfall.
apple_scab.favorable_conditions: Cool (13-24°C), wet spring weather requiring prolonged leaf wetness (6-24 hours).
prevention: Rake and destroy or chop fallen leaves in autumn to reduce primary inoculum.
Prune tree canopy annually to facilitate rapid leaf drying and sunlight penetration.
Plant resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Freedom, Prima).
management: Apply protective bio-fungicides or sulfur sprays during early green-tip through petal fall.
Consult local university extension spray calendars for degree-day infection models.
apple_scab.consult_expert_when: Scab lesions appear on flower clusters or fruitlets.
apple_scab.references: Cornell AgriTech Apple Scab Guidelines; Penn State Tree Fruit Production Guide.

black_rot.symptoms: Small purple spots on upper leaf surfaces that enlarge into circular lesions with light brown centers and purple borders (frogeye pattern).
black_rot.causes: Overwinters in dead wood, mummified fruits, and cankers on twigs.
prevention: Prune out dead wood, cankered limbs, and fire-blight strikes during winter.
Remove all mummified apples hanging from trees.
Avoid wounding bark during orchard operations.
management: Maintain thorough orchard sanitation.
Apply targeted protective sprays if history of orchard infection is documented.
black_rot.consult_expert_when: Cankers expand around main scaffold limbs.
black_rot.references: Penn State Extension Fruit Pathology; University of Kentucky Plant Pathology.

cedar_apple_rust.symptoms: Bright yellow-orange or red circular spots on upper leaf surface. Small black dots (pycnia) form in center, followed by tube-like aecia on lower surface.
cedar_apple_rust.causes: Obligate heteroecious rust fungus alternating between eastern red cedar/juniper and apple trees.
cedar_apple_rust.favorable_conditions: Wet spring periods when cedar galls swell and release gelatinous telial horns.
prevention: Remove nearby wild red cedar trees within 500 meters of the orchard where feasible.
Plant rust-immune or resistant varieties (e.g., Enterprise, Liberty).
Inspect nearby ornamental junipers for galls in late winter.
management: Apply protective fungicides from pink-bud until 2-3 weeks after petal-fall if cedar trees are nearby.
cedar_apple_rust.consult_expert_when: Severe defoliation occurs on susceptible honeycrisp or gala trees.

healthy.symptoms: Uniform deep green foliage, crisp margins, and absence of pustules, spots, or powdery growth.
healthy.causes: Good pruning, balanced nutrition, and clean orchard floor.
prevention: Maintain routine dormant pruning, soil testing, and seasonal monitoring.
management: Follow standard orchard maintenance guidelines.
healthy.consult_expert_when: Report unexpected leaf drop or pest infestations.
healthy.references: Penn State Tree Fruit Production Guide.

black_rot.symptoms: Reddish-brown circular spots on leaves that enlarge and develop dark borders with tiny black specks (pycnidia) arranged in rings.
black_rot.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (21-32°C) combined with high rainfall or prolonged dew.
prevention: Remove mummified berries and infected canes during dormant pruning.
Trellis vines to encourage rapid air circulation and canopy drying.
Keep vineyard floor mowed.
management: Apply protective fungicides from 10 cm shoot growth through veraison.
black_rot.consult_expert_when: Infection spreads to grape berry clusters.
black_rot.references: UC Davis IPM Grape Pest Management Guidelines; Cornell Extension.

esca_black_measles.symptoms: 'Tiger-striped' chlorotic and necrotic patterns between leaf veins; sudden apoplexy (vine collapse) in hot midsummer.
esca_black_measles.causes: Vascular wood rot fungi penetrating through winter pruning wounds.
esca_black_measles.favorable_conditions: Mature vineyards (>8-10 years old), drought stress, followed by sudden heat waves.
prevention: Delay pruning until late winter to minimize spore infection.
Seal large pruning wounds with wound sealants or biocontrol Trichoderma.
Disinfect pruning shears with 70% alcohol or bleach solution between vines.
management: Trunk renewal or remedial surgery on symptomatic arms.
Mark infected vines in summer for targeted winter treatment.
esca_black_measles.consult_expert_when: Entire cordons or whole vines collapse suddenly.
esca_black_measles.references: UC IPM Grapevine Trunk Diseases; INRAE Viticulture Research.

leaf_blight.symptoms: Irregular large brown or reddish-brown lesions with distinct dark borders, leading to premature leaf drop in late season.
leaf_blight.causes: Overwintering fungal mycelium in fallen vine debris.
leaf_blight.favorable_conditions: Humid, dense canopies with low sunlight penetration in late summer.
prevention: Canopy leaf thinning around the fruiting zone.
Dispose of autumn leaf litter.
management: Ensure adequate potassium nutrition and avoid excess irrigation late in season.
leaf_blight.references: Cornell Viticulture Notes; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension.

healthy.symptoms: Lush green, well-expanded leaves without vein banding, necrosis, or fungal sporulation.
healthy.causes: Balanced canopy management and disease-free rootstocks.
healthy.favorable_conditions: Well-drained vineyard soil with good solar exposure.
prevention: Maintain seasonal shoot positioning and routine canopy scouting.
management: Standard vineyard nutrient and irrigation schedule.
healthy.consult_expert_when: Scout regularly during bloom and bunch closure.

bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small (2-3 mm) dark brown water-soaked circular spots, often surrounded by a yellow halo. Spots may coalesce, causing blighted leaf margins.
bacterial_spot.causes: Contaminated seeds, transplants, or wind-driven rain splashing from crop residue.
bacterial_spot.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24-30°C) and persistent rain or overhead sprinkler irrigation.
prevention: Use certified pathogen-free seed and transplants.
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation at ground level.
Rotate fields away from solanaceous crops for at least 2 years.
management: Apply preventative copper-based sprays combined with mancozeb as recommended by extension.
Do not work in fields when foliage is wet to avoid spreading bacteria.
bacterial_spot.consult_expert_when: Foliage blighting exceeds 15% and affects developing green fruits.
bacterial_spot.references: University of Florida IFAS Extension; Cornell Vegetable MD Online.

early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown circular spots with characteristic concentric rings ('target board' pattern) on older lower leaves, surrounded by yellow chlorosis.
early_blight.causes: Soil-borne fungal spores splashed onto lower leaves during rainfall or irrigation.
early_blight.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24-29°C) with alternating wet and dry weather.
prevention: Mulch around plant bases to prevent soil splashing onto foliage.
Prune bottom 30 cm of foliage to improve ventilation.
Stake and trellis tomato vines off the ground.
management: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves immediately upon first detection.
Apply protective biofungicides or copper sulfate according to label.
early_blight.consult_expert_when: Concentric lesions spread to upper leaves or stem collars.
early_blight.references: Penn State Extension Tomato Pathology; Purdue Extension.

late_blight.symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked pale green or dark brown lesions. In humid weather, white cottony fungal-like growth appears on underside of leaves.
late_blight.causes: Wind-borne sporangia; catastrophic historical plant disease capable of killing plants within days.
prevention: Plant certified resistant varieties (e.g., Defiant, Mountain Magic, Iron Lady).
Eliminate volunteer tomato and potato plants from vicinity.
Avoid planting tomatoes adjacent to potato patches.
management: Immediate removal and bagging of severely infected plants to prevent airborne spore clouds.
Report outbreaks to regional agricultural extension monitors.
late_blight.consult_expert_when: Urgent notification to local agricultural authorities recommended immediately.
late_blight.references: USAblight National Warning System; Cornell University Plant Pathology.

septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Numerous small (2-3 mm) circular spots with grayish-white centers and dark brown margins. Tiny black speckles (pycnidia) clearly visible in center.
septoria_leaf_spot.causes: Fungus overwintering in Solanaceae weed hosts (e.g., horsenettle) and crop debris.
septoria_leaf_spot.favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (20-25°C) with high humidity and rain.
prevention: 3-year crop rotation without nightshade crops.
Bottom pruning and clean straw mulching.
Weed management of solanaceous weeds around field borders.
management: Strip infected lower leaves as soon as detected.
Maintain drip irrigation and promote good airflow.
septoria_leaf_spot.consult_expert_when: Rapid defoliation threatens sunscald on ripening fruits.
septoria_leaf_spot.references: Missouri Botanical Garden Pest Advice; Ohio State Extension.

healthy.symptoms: Deep green compound leaves, robust petioles, without spots, chlorosis, or curling.
healthy.causes: Well-balanced nitrogen/potassium, adequate soil moisture, and pest exclusion.
healthy.favorable_conditions: Sunny, warm growing season with well-drained fertile loam.
prevention: Maintain routine scouting, staking, and drip watering.
management: Continue integrated nutrient and pest management.
healthy.consult_expert_when: Monitor weekly for aphids, hornworms, or early leaf spots.
healthy.references: UC IPM Tomato Pest Management Guidelines.

early_blight.symptoms: Circular to angular dark brown lesions with concentric rings, restricted by major leaf veins. Yellowing around lesions leads to premature leaf senescence.
early_blight.causes: Overwinters on infected potato debris or tubers.
early_blight.favorable_conditions: High humidity alternating with warm dry periods.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers.
Maintain optimal soil nitrogen and phosphorus levels to prevent vine stress.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (grains, corn, legumes).
management: Apply protective fungicides when symptoms first emerge on lower leaves.
Ensure uniform irrigation to avoid vine stress.
early_blight.consult_expert_when: Lesions begin coalescing across mid-canopy foliage.
early_blight.references: University of Idaho Potato Pathology; North Dakota State Extension.

late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked irregular black/brown lesions starting at leaf tips or margins. White downy sporulation visible on leaf undersides in humid conditions. Causes foul odor.
late_blight.causes: Infected seed tubers or cull piles.
late_blight.favorable_conditions: Cool nights (10-15°C) and warm days (15-21°C) with persistent humidity >90%.
prevention: Destroy all cull piles and volunteer potato sprouts before planting season.
Plant certified resistant varieties.
Hill up soil well around tubers to prevent spore wash-down.
management: Immediate fungicide application following local late blight forecast models.
Kill vines before harvest to prevent tuber contamination.
late_blight.consult_expert_when: Immediate consultation with agricultural extension required upon detection.
late_blight.references: International Potato Center (CIP); University of Wisconsin Extension.

healthy.symptoms: Broad green leaflets with smooth margins, absence of black lesions or fungal down.
healthy.causes: Healthy seed tubers and clean soil.
healthy.favorable_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures and balanced soil nutrition.
prevention: Scout fields twice weekly during flowering and tuber bulking.
management: Follow scheduled hilling and integrated pest management.
healthy.consult_expert_when: Investigate immediately if sudden dark lesions appear.

cercospora_leaf_spot.disease_name: Gray Leaf Spot / Cercospora Leaf Spot
cercospora_leaf_spot.symptoms: Small rectangular tan or gray spots strictly delimited by leaf veins ('blocky' shape), running parallel to leaf veins.
cercospora_leaf_spot.causes: Overwinters in corn residue on soil surface; conidia spread by wind and rain splash.
cercospora_leaf_spot.favorable_conditions: Extended periods of high relative humidity (>90%) and warm temperatures (24-32°C).
prevention: Select corn hybrids with high Gray Leaf Spot resistance ratings.
Rotate crops with soybeans, wheat, or alfalfa.
Implement conservation tillage practices that incorporate residue where suitable.
management: Foliar fungicide application between VT and R1 growth stages if threshold is exceeded.
Maintain balanced soil fertility.
cercospora_leaf_spot.consult_expert_when: Lesions reach the ear leaf or above prior to blister stage (R2).
cercospora_leaf_spot.references: Purdue University Extension Corn Disease Series; Iowa State Extension.

common_rust.symptoms: Oval to elongated golden-brown or cinnamon-brown pustules scattered across both upper and lower leaf surfaces. Pustules rupture the epidermis to release powdery spores.
common_rust.causes: Wind-borne urediniospores blown from southern production regions.
common_rust.favorable_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (16-25°C) and high humidity with 6-8 hours of dew.
prevention: Plant resistant corn hybrids carrying Rp gene resistance.
Early planting to avoid peak midsummer spore showers.
management: Most commercial hybrids exhibit partial resistance; fungicide rarely needed unless susceptible inbred lines.
common_rust.consult_expert_when: Rust pustules cover >10% of ear leaf area before silking.
common_rust.references: University of Illinois Field Crop Pathology; CIMMYT Maize Guide.

northern_leaf_blight.symptoms: Large, elongated cigar-shaped or elliptical grayish-green to tan lesions (2.5-15 cm long). Dark fungal sporulation visible within lesions in damp weather.
northern_leaf_blight.causes: Fungus overwintering in corn crop debris.
northern_leaf_blight.favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (18-27°C) with persistent wet foliage.
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids carrying Ht resistance genes.
One to two year crop rotation away from corn.
Residue management.
management: Foliar fungicide application if lesions appear on third leaf below ear or higher before silking.
northern_leaf_blight.references: CIMMYT Maize Pathology; University of Nebraska-Lincoln Extension.

healthy.symptoms: Long, arched green leaf blades without brown pustules, blights, or necrotic streaks.
healthy.causes: Optimal hybrid selection and balanced macro/micronutrient uptake.
healthy.favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days with adequate soil moisture.
prevention: Scout weekly during vegetative growth through tasseling.
management: Standard fertilizer side-dressing and weed control.
healthy.consult_expert_when: Inspect if unexpected chlorotic striping or wilting occurs.

healthy.symptoms: Firm, intact skin with uniform varietal pigmentation, no soft spots, skin ruptures, or fungal sporulation.
healthy.causes: Optimal orchard maturity, careful harvest handling, and controlled post-harvest storage.
healthy.favorable_conditions: Cold storage at 0-2°C with 90-95% relative humidity and controlled atmosphere.
prevention: Maintain cold chain promptly after harvesting; minimize mechanical bruising during grading and packing.
management: Store at recommended temperature and monitor ethylene concentrations.
healthy.consult_expert_when: Rapid softening or internal browning occurs in cold storage.
healthy.references: UC Davis Postharvest Technology Center; USDA-ARS Apple Handling Guidelines.

minor_blemish.symptoms: Superficial corky russeting, minor sunburn patches, or light limb-rub marks without deep flesh decay or foul odor.
minor_blemish.causes: High humidity or frost during fruitlet development, pesticide phytotoxicity, or mechanical rubbing by adjacent branches.
minor_blemish.favorable_conditions: Wet spring mornings during early cell division stage; wind exposure.
prevention: Avoid phytotoxic chemical applications in wet weather during bloom to petal-fall.
Install orchard windbreaks and prune rubbing branches.
management: Sort affected fruit for secondary processing (cider, applesauce) or immediate consumption; fruit flesh remains edible.
minor_blemish.consult_expert_when: Blemishes turn soft, sunken, or exude liquid indicative of secondary fungal infection.
minor_blemish.references: Cornell Cooperative Extension Tree Fruit IPM; Penn State Extension Apple Diseases.

rot_decay.symptoms: Soft, watery circular brown rot lesions that rapidly expand and sink into the flesh. Blue-green or gray spore masses emerge on the surface, producing a moldy odor.
rot_decay.causes: Infection through skin punctures, stem pulls, or insect feeding injuries during harvest and storage.
rot_decay.favorable_conditions: Warm ambient temperatures (>15°C) and high humidity on injured fruit surfaces.
prevention: Avoid rough handling, stem punctures, and overfilling harvest bins.
Sanitize dump tanks, flumes, and packing line contact surfaces regularly.
Cool fruit immediately to 0°C within 24 hours of harvest.
management: Cull rotten fruit immediately to prevent nest rots and airborne spore spread in storage bins.
Do not use moldy apples for juice due to patulin mycotoxin risks.
rot_decay.consult_expert_when: Widespread decay exceeds 5% of stored fruit bins.
rot_decay.references: Washington State University Tree Fruit Postharvest Pathology; USDA Postharvest Pathology.

healthy.symptoms: Firm fruit fingers with smooth, clean green or yellow peel, intact pedicels, and no sunken necrotic lesions.
healthy.causes: Adequate bunch covering, proper maturity harvest (3/4 full), and ethylene-controlled ripening.
healthy.favorable_conditions: Storage at 13-14°C with 85-90% relative humidity. Avoid temperatures below 12°C to prevent chilling injury.
prevention: Use bunch bags in the field; handle fruit gently with foam padding in packing stations.
management: Maintain temperature between 13°C and 18°C during ripening.
healthy.consult_expert_when: Peel discoloration occurs without temperature or ripening protocol deviations.
healthy.references: FAO Banana Post-Harvest Handling Guide; UC Davis Postharvest Technology.

minor_blemish.symptoms: Small brown speckles ('sugar spots') indicating peak ripeness, or minor latex staining/light abrasion marks on the peel surface. Fruit pulp is sweet and intact.
minor_blemish.causes: Natural ripening enzymatic activity converting starches to simple sugars; latex exudate contact during de-handing.
minor_blemish.favorable_conditions: Advanced ripeness stage (Color Stage 6-7) at room temperature.
prevention: Rinse harvested hands in de-latexing water baths containing alum.
Distribute promptly before over-ripening.
management: Consume or process promptly for baking, smoothies, or dehydration.
minor_blemish.consult_expert_when: Peel softens into blackened watery tissue penetrating through to the pulp.
minor_blemish.references: Queensland Department of Agriculture and Fisheries Banana Postharvest Management.

rot_decay.symptoms: Black, sunken rotting lesions on peel surfaces and cushion/crown tissues. Lesions coalesce into large necrotic blotches with salmon-pink or black fungal sporulation, causing pulp breakdown.
rot_decay.causes: Latent fungal infections established in the plantation that develop as fruit ripens and peel resistance declines.
rot_decay.favorable_conditions: High humidity (>90%), warm temperatures (22-28°C), and physical injuries to peel or crown.
prevention: Apply field bunch sanitation and de-flower before bagging.
Sanitize de-handing knives and packing water baths.
Dry crowns thoroughly before packing into ventilated cartons.
management: Separate and discard infected clusters to avoid cross-contamination in packing boxes.
Ensure prompt cooling and avoid elevated humidity in retail displays.
rot_decay.consult_expert_when: Decay rates exceed acceptable retail threshold (>3% of cartons affected).
rot_decay.references: Bioversity International Banana Pathology; University of Hawaii CTAHR Extension.

healthy.symptoms: Firm, turgid rind with uniform color break, intact oil glands, smooth calyx (button), and no soft decay or water-soaked spots.
healthy.causes: Optimal irrigation, balanced potassium nutrition, and careful harvesting using fruit clippers.
healthy.favorable_conditions: Storage at 4-7°C with 90-95% relative humidity and proper ventilation.
prevention: Clip fruit rather than pulling to avoid stem-end rind tears; harvest only dry trees.
management: Store at 5-7°C and maintain sanitation across packing lines.
healthy.consult_expert_when: Premature fruit drop or calyx yellowing occurs in storage.
healthy.references: University of Florida IFAS Citrus Extension; UC Davis Postharvest Technology.

minor_blemish.disease_name: Superficial Citrus Rind Blemish / Thrips Scarring
minor_blemish.symptoms: Smooth, grayish-silvery rings or patches around the stem end, or light corky rind streaks without soft decay or internal pulp injury.
minor_blemish.causes: Flower thrips feeding on young fruitlets or gentle wind whipping against twigs during early fruit development.
minor_blemish.favorable_conditions: Dry spring weather during petal-fall through fruit sizing (under 3 cm diameter).
prevention: Monitor thrips populations during bloom and apply selective bio-insecticides if threshold exceeded.
Maintain perimeter windbreaks.
management: Sort for fresh retail or grade for juicing; internal juice vesicles and quality are unaffected.
minor_blemish.consult_expert_when: Rind spots become raised, dark brown, or exhibit concentric fungal rings.
minor_blemish.references: University of California Citrus IPM Guidelines; Florida Citrus Postharvest Handling Guide.

rot_decay.symptoms: Soft, water-soaked, circular lesion on the rind that easily punctures under finger pressure. Dense white mycelium rapidly develops, followed by olive-green or blue-green powdery spore masses surrounded by a white margin.
rot_decay.causes: Wound pathogen entering microscopic rind punctures, fingernail scratches, or oleocellosis injuries.
rot_decay.favorable_conditions: Temperatures of 20-25°C, high humidity, and rind injuries during harvest.
prevention: Harvest fruit with cotton gloves; sanitize picking clippers and field lugs.
Sanitize packing line wash water with food-grade peracetic acid or chlorine dioxide.
Apply edible wax coatings to seal micro-wounds.
management: Isolate and discard decaying fruit immediately to prevent spore clouds from contaminating adjacent sound fruit.
Lower storage temperature to 4-6°C to slow fungal germination.
rot_decay.consult_expert_when: Decay spreads across packed cartons in cold transit.
rot_decay.references: University of Florida Citrus Extension; USDA-ARS Citrus Pathology Research.

bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, circular to irregular water-soaked spots on foliage turning dark brown with pale yellow halos. Lesions cause premature leaf defoliation, exposing fruit to sunscald.
bacterial_spot.causes: Seedborne bacterium or splash dispersal from infected crop residues and volunteer solanaceous weeds.
bacterial_spot.favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (24-30°C) with persistent high humidity, dew, and overhead sprinkler irrigation.
prevention: Use certified disease-free hot-water-treated pepper seeds.
Practice a minimum 2-year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops.
Avoid overhead irrigation to minimize canopy leaf wetness duration.
management: Apply preventative copper-mancozeb tank mixes according to regional extension recommendations.
Remove and destroy severely blighted plants during early localized outbreaks.
bacterial_spot.consult_expert_when: Defoliation spreads across >15% of plants before flowering.
bacterial_spot.references: University of Florida IFAS Extension Pepper Disease Guide; UC Davis Vegetable IPM.

healthy.symptoms: Uniform deep green leaf canopy without necrotic spotting, yellowing margins, mosaic mottling, or defoliation.
healthy.causes: Optimal nutrient management and balanced drip irrigation without active pathogen vectors.
healthy.favorable_conditions: Sunny, warm conditions with good air circulation.
prevention: Scout fields bi-weekly and maintain preventative weed sanitation around field perimeters.
management: Maintain balanced potassium-to-nitrogen ratios and continue scouting.
healthy.consult_expert_when: Inspect if unexpected leaf curling or chlorotic mottling occurs.
healthy.references: World Vegetable Center (AVRDC) Pepper Production Guidelines.
